claim: Respiratory droplets and aerosols have been demonstrated as a major route of transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: While respiratory droplets and aerosols have rapidly been demonstrated as a major route of transmission of SARS-CoV-2 (Tang et al., 2020), the role of the viral load as a driver of infectiousness has been established (He et al., 2020) but not quantified.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2020

claim: The role of viral load as a driver of infectiousness has been established but not quantified.
source: While respiratory droplets and aerosols have rapidly been demonstrated as a major route of transmission of SARS-CoV-2 (Tang et al., 2020), the role of the viral load as a driver of infectiousness has been established (He et al., 2020) but not quantified.
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2020 and statement about lack of quantification

claim: High-risk contacts occur mostly before the index has been diagnosed, with no information on the viral load level at the time of the contact.
source: This lack of evidence is due to the fact that high-risk contacts occur mostly before the index has been diagnosed, with no information on the viral load level at the time of the contact.
evidence: Statement about timing of contacts relative to diagnosis

claim: Variants of concern are associated with larger viral loads.
source: In the context of variants of concern, that are associated with larger viral loads (Teyssou et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Elie et al., 2021; Cosentino et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2021), it becomes even more critical to delineate the contribution of viral load from other factors associated with an increased transmission.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on variants

claim: Antiviral drugs and vaccine strategies dramatically reduce the amount of viral shedding.
source: Further, as antiviral drugs and vaccine strategies are being implemented, that dramatically reduce the amount of viral shedding (Levine-Tiefenbrun et al., 2021), it is essential to understand how they may contribute to a reduction in virus transmission.
evidence: Supported by citation to Levine-Tiefenbrun et al., 2021

claim: A randomised controlled trial was conducted in March-April 2020 in Spain to assess the efficacy of hydroxychloroquine on SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: One of the most documented clinical study to address the question of viral load and infectiousness has been obtained through individuals included in a randomised controlled trial conducted in March-April 2020 in Spain, that aimed to assess the efficacy of hydroxychloroquine on SARS-CoV-2 transmission (Mitjà et al., 2021; Marks et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitjà et al., 2021 and Marks et al., 2021

claim: 282 index cases and their 753 high-risk contacts were frequently monitored to assess their virological and clinical evolution.
source: Overall, 282 index and their 753 high-risk contacts were frequently monitored to assess their virological and clinical evolution.
evidence: Statement about study design and sample size

claim: An association was found between the probability of being infected after a high-risk contact and the viral load measured at the time of diagnosis in the index case.
source: An association was found between the probability of being infected after a high-risk contact and the viral load measured at the time of diagnosis in the index case (Marks et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marks et al., 2021

claim: 259 index cases and their 582 high-risk contacts were included in the analysis.
source: A total of 259 index cases and their 582 high-risk contacts (simply called contacts in the following) were included in our analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement about final sample size with reference to figure

claim: The majority of index cases were female (72%) with a median age of 42.
source: The majority of index cases were female (72%) with a median age of 42 (90% Inter Quantile Range (IQR): [24, 61]).
evidence: Descriptive statistics from the study population

claim: A total of 544 swab samples were performed at days 0, 3 and 7 days after study inclusion.
source: A total of 544 swab samples were performed at days 0, 3 and 7 days after study inclusion.

claim: The first swab was performed after a median time of 4 days after symptom onset.
source: The first swab was performed after a median time of 4 days (90% IQR: [2, 6]) after symptom onset.

claim: The maximum median viral load obtained during follow-up was 8.4 log10 copies per mL.
source: The maximum median viral load obtained during follow-up was 8.4 log10 copies per mL (90% IQR:[5.1, 10.6]).
evidence: Descriptive statistics from viral load measurements

claim: The majority of contacts were female (56%) with a median age of 41.
source: The majority of contacts were female (56%) with a median age of 41 (90% IQR: [20, 65]).
evidence: Descriptive statistics from the study population

claim: 60% of contacts were household contacts and 40% were non-household contacts.
source: The form of contacts was categorized as either household (60%) or non-household (40%).

claim: 87 household contacts led to an infection with a proportion of transmission of 24.9%.
source: Overall, 87 household contact led to an infection (proportion of transmission of 24.9%) and 29 non-household contacts led to an infection (proportion of transmission of 12.4%).

claim: 29 non-household contacts led to an infection with a proportion of transmission of 12.4%.
source: Overall, 87 household contact led to an infection (proportion of transmission of 24.9%) and 29 non-household contacts led to an infection (proportion of transmission of 12.4%).

claim: The majority of contacts (65%) and of infection events (65%) occurred ±1 day from symptom onset of the index cases.
source: The majority of contacts (65%) and of infection events (65%) occurred ±1 day from symptom onset of the index cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Descriptive statistics with reference to figure

claim: The incubation period has a log-normal distribution with a mean value of 5 days.
source: We used a target cell limited model to reconstruct the viral load kinetics of the index cases over time, assuming that the incubation period has a log-normal distribution with a mean value of 5 days (Néant et al., 2021; Lauer et al., 2020).

claim: The model predicted that the median peak viral load coincided with symptom onset, with a median peak value of 9.4 log10 copies per mL.
source: When reconstructing the viral load profiles, the model predicted that the median peak viral load coincided with symptom onset, with a median peak value of 9.4 log10 copies per mL (90% IQR: [8.0, 10.0]).
evidence: Model prediction based on fitted parameters

claim: Models assuming an effect of viral load on the probability of transmission (Model M2 and M3) provided an improvement in BIC compared to the model without viral load effect (Model M1).
source: The two model assuming an effect of viral load on the probability of transmission (Model M2 and M3) provided an improvement in BIC as compared to the model M1, supporting an effect of viral load on the probability of infection.

claim: Viral load was significantly associated with the probability of transmission after household contact (p<0.01).
source: In both models, viral load was significantly associated with the probability of transmission after household contact (p<0.01, Wald test on γ1); however, the effect was lower after non-household transmission (p<0.05, Wald test on γ2).
evidence: Statistical test result from model fitting

claim: The effect of viral load on transmission was lower after non-household transmission (p<0.05).
source: In both models, viral load was significantly associated with the probability of transmission after household contact (p<0.01, Wald test on γ1); however, the effect was lower after non-household transmission (p<0.05, Wald test on γ2).
evidence: Statistical test result from model fitting

claim: The probability of transmission was fixed to 5% for viral load levels below six log10 copies/mL, which is generally the threshold for virus culture in vitro.
source: Because we fixed the probability of transmission to 5% for viral load levels below six log10 copies/mL, which is generally the threshold for virus culture in vitro (Jones et al., 2021; Néant et al., 2021; van Kampen et al., 2021; Mollan et al., 2021), we tested models with threshold values ranging from 4 to 8 log10 copies/mL and they all yielded similar results (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Model assumption supported by citations to virus culture studies

claim: The mean probability of transmission increased from 5% for viral load levels < 6 log10 copies per mL to 48% for viral load ≥ 10 log10 copies per mL for household contacts.
source: The model predicted that the mean probability of transmission increased from the fixed nominal value of 5% for viral load levels < 6 log10 copies per mL, to as much as 48% and 20% for viral load ≥ 10 log10 copies per mL for household and non-household contacts, respectively.
evidence: Model prediction based on fitted parameters

claim: The mean probability of transmission increased from 5% for viral load levels < 6 log10 copies per mL to 20% for viral load ≥ 10 log10 copies per mL for non-household contacts.
source: The model predicted that the mean probability of transmission increased from the fixed nominal value of 5% for viral load levels < 6 log10 copies per mL, to as much as 48% and 20% for viral load ≥ 10 log10 copies per mL for household and non-household contacts, respectively.
evidence: Model prediction based on fitted parameters

claim: The median probability of transmission peaked at the time of symptom onset with a mean value of 29% in household contacts.
source: Over the time of infection, the median probability of transmission peaked at the time of symptom onset with a mean value of 29% in household contacts.

claim: At the peak of transmission in household contacts, there was large inter-individual variability with a 90% inter quantile range of 6-96%.
source: However, there was large inter-individual variabilities due to both viral load levels and individual characteristics, with a 90% inter quantile range of 6-96% (Figure 3).

claim: The peak of transmission was much lower in non-household contacts, with a mean value of 13%.
source: The peak of transmission was much lower in non-household contacts, with a mean value of 13% (90% IQR: [5, 38]).

claim: The probability of transmission was above 5% for a median duration of 12 days.
source: The probability of transmission was above 5% for a median duration of 12 days (90% IQR: [9, 15]).

claim: The median generation interval was estimated to be 5.1 days for household contacts when a time-varying rate of contacts was used.
source: The median generation interval was estimated to be 5.1 days (90% IQR: [1, 10]) and 4.8 days (90% IQR: [1, 11]) for household and non-household contacts respectively, when a time-varying rate of contacts was used.

claim: The median generation interval was estimated to be 4.8 days for non-household contacts when a time-varying rate of contacts was used.
source: The median generation interval was estimated to be 5.1 days (90% IQR: [1, 10]) and 4.8 days (90% IQR: [1, 11]) for household and non-household contacts respectively, when a time-varying rate of contacts was used.

claim: The generation interval estimates are close to what has been found in other studies.
source: Those estimates are close, albeit with higher variability, to what has been found in other studies (Cereda et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with literature supported by citations

claim: For the baseline scenario, the average transmission probability was 18% for household contacts and 9% for non-household contacts.
source: For the baseline scenario using the parameters estimated in our population, the average transmission probability was 18% and 9% for household and non-household contacts, respectively.

claim: With a twofold increase in viral production (corresponding to B1.1.7 strain), the average probability of transmission would increase to 22% for household contacts and 11% for non-household contacts.
source: With an increased value of viral production, p, by a factor 2, which corresponds to the viral load increase caused by B1.1.7 strain in large-scale epidemiological studies (Golubchik et al., 2021; Roquebert et al., 2021; Kidd et al., 2021), the average probability of transmission would increase to 22% and 11% for household and non-household contacts respectively.
evidence: Model prediction based on variant data from literature

claim: With a fourfold increase in viral production, the average probability of transmission would increase to 26% for household contacts and 12% for non-household contacts.
source: With a fourfold increase, as suggested elsewhere (Teyssou et al., 2021), the average probability of transmission would increase to 26% and 12% for household and non-household contacts, respectively (Figure 4C).
evidence: Model prediction based on variant data from literature

claim: Assuming an eightfold increase in viral load, the average probability of transmission would increase to 29% for household contacts and 13% for non-household contacts.
source: Assuming an increase by eightfold of the viral load, the average probability of transmission would increase to 29% and 13% for household and non-household contacts, respectively.
evidence: Model prediction based on variant data

claim: A two-, four-, or eightfold increase in viral production rate would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% for household contacts.
source: As compared to the results observed with the historical virus a two-, four-, or eightfold increase in viral production rate would therefore lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% for household contacts, and of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contacts (Figure 4D).

claim: A two-, four-, or eightfold increase in viral production rate would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contacts.
source: As compared to the results observed with the historical virus a two-, four-, or eightfold increase in viral production rate would therefore lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% for household contacts, and of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contacts (Figure 4D).

claim: Epidemiological studies in Israel reported a 3-5-fold lower viral load in infected vaccinated individuals compared to unvaccinated individuals.
source: Epidemiological studies in Israel reported a 3-5-fold lower viral load in infected vaccinated individuals as compared to unvaccinated individuals (Levine-Tiefenbrun et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levine-Tiefenbrun et al., 2021

claim: Some studies relying on systematic repeated viral testing reported a 30-100-fold reduction in viral load levels with vaccination.
source: In other studies relying on systematic repeated viral testing in both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals, the effect of vaccine was much more dramatic, with a 30-100-fold reduction in viral load levels (McEllistrem et al., 2021; Thompson et al., 2021; Bailly et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Assuming a 16-fold reduction in viral load, the average probability of transmission would decrease to its nominal value of 5% for both household and non-household contacts.
source: Assuming a reduction of 16-fold (~4 Ct) of the viral load, the average probability of transmission would decrease to its nominal value of 5% for both household and non-household contacts.

claim: A 4- or 16-fold reduction in viral production rate would lead to a relative decrease in the average transmission probability of 61% or 72% for household contacts.
source: As compared to the results observed with the historical virus, a 4- or 16-fold reduction in viral production rate would lead to a relative decrease in the average transmission probability of 61% or 72% for household contacts and of 38 or 47% for non-household contacts.

claim: A 4- or 16-fold reduction in viral production rate would lead to a relative decrease in the average transmission probability of 38% or 47% for non-household contacts.
source: As compared to the results observed with the historical virus, a 4- or 16-fold reduction in viral production rate would lead to a relative decrease in the average transmission probability of 61% or 72% for household contacts and of 38 or 47% for non-household contacts.

claim: The effect of viral load was particularly large in household contacts, with a mean transmission probability that increased to as much as 48% when the viral load was over 10 log10 copies per mL.
source: Here, we quantified the impact of viral load on infectiousness using data obtained in a prospective cohorts of index and contact cases (Mitjà et al., 2021). The effect of viral load was particularly large in household contacts, with a mean transmission probability that increased to as much as 48% when the viral load was over 10 log10 copies per mL.

claim: The effect of viral load on transmission was individual-dependent.
source: Consistent with reports suggesting that the probability of transmission (Edwards et al., 2021) greatly vary between individuals, the effect of viral load was individual-dependent.

claim: At the peak of infectiousness, the mean probability of transmission during household contact was 29% with a 90% inter quantile range of 6–96%.
source: For instance, at the peak of infectiousness, the mean probability of transmission during household contact was 29% with a 90% inter quantile range of 6–96%.

claim: Large-scale epidemiological data reported an average increase of the B1.1.7 virus by 1-2 Ct.
source: We relied on results found in both large-scale epidemiological data and longitudinal evaluation of Ct values (Elie et al., 2021; Cosentino et al., 2021), that reported an average increase of the B1.1.7 virus by 1-2 Ct (Teyssou et al., 2021; Golubchik et al., 2021; Roquebert et al., 2021), which can be reproduced in our model by assuming that viral production increases by a factor 2-4.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies

claim: The N501Y substitution improved the affinity of the viral spike protein.
source: Alternatively, as only the product p × T0 can be identified, this could also be due to B1.1.7 being able to infect twice as much target cells, as suggested by the fact that the N501Y substitution improved the affinity of the viral spike protein (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021

claim: An increase of viral load by a factor of 2, 4, or 8 would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% in household contacts.
source: Regardless of the origin of this increased viral load, we estimated that an increase of viral load by a factor of 2, 4, or 8 would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% in household contacts and of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contact.

claim: An increase of viral load by a factor of 2, 4, or 8 would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contacts.
source: Regardless of the origin of this increased viral load, we estimated that an increase of viral load by a factor of 2, 4, or 8 would lead to a relative increase in the average transmission probability of 24, 42, or 58% in household contacts and of 15, 27, or 39% for non-household contact.

claim: Another modelling study performed in a small population of frequently sampled individuals diagnosed early in their infection did not find an effect of B1.1.7 on viral kinetics.
source: In fact, another modelling study performed in a small population of frequently sampled individuals diagnosed early in their infection did not find an effect of B1.1.7 on viral kinetics (Ke et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ke et al., 2021

claim: The exact magnitude of viral load decrease with vaccination depends on the design of the study.
source: The exact magnitude of this decrease is difficult to quantify, and depends on the design of the study that relied on systematic testing or included only symptomatic individuals.
evidence: Discussion of methodological factors affecting estimates

claim: Reductions of fourfold or more in viral load will dramatically reduce the probability of transmission carried by vaccinated infected individuals.
source: Whatever the exact value, our predictions indicate that reductions of fourfold or more will dramatically reduce the probability of transmission carried by vaccinated infected individuals.

claim: At the time the study was conducted, the role of pre-symptomatic transmission was not known.
source: One of them is the fact that at the time where the study was conducted, the role of pre-symptomatic transmission was not known.
evidence: Statement about knowledge at time of study

claim: It is possible that recollection bias leads to an overestimation of contacts reporting on the day of symptom onset.
source: Also, it is possible that recollection bias leads to an overestimation of contacts reporting on the day of symptom onset.

claim: The study was conducted during the first epidemic wave in Spain, where most individuals had not yet applied social distancing and masking.
source: Indeed, the study was conducted during the first epidemic wave in Spain, where most individuals, including in hospital settings, had not yet applied social distancing and masking, causing dozens of thousands of individuals infected every day.

claim: Viral load data in index cases were collected on average 3–4 days after symptom onset, in the declining phase of viral load.
source: It is also important to note that viral load data in index cases were collected on average 3–4 days after symptom onset, in the declining phase of viral load, several days after most of the contacts had occurred.

claim: The peak viral load coincides with symptom onset in SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: This limitation is inherent to the nature of SARS-CoV-2, where the peak viral load coincides with symptom onset, making difficult to obtain data during the replicating phase of the virus where individuals are largely asymptomatic.

claim: In the original analysis, the use of face mask by contacts was not found associated with a decreased viral load.
source: In the original analysis of Marks et al., 2021, the use of face mask by contacts was not found associated with a decreased viral load, but this probably reflects the lack of more detailed data on the type of mask, the use of other personal protective equipment and infection control practices.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marks et al., 2021 with interpretation

claim: Face masking was poorly reported and was missing in about 35% of contacts.
source: It is also important to recall that face masking was poorly reported and was missing in about 35% of contacts, limiting statistical power (Supplementary file 4).

claim: The use of face mask by index cases has a far more substantial effect on viral shedding and thus on transmission than mask use by contacts.
source: This information might be of a greater importance as it has a far more substantial effect on viral shedding and thus on transmission.
evidence: Statement about relative importance of mask use

claim: Two- to eightfold increase in viral load level observed with variants of concern could lead to an increase in the probability of transmission by 24–58% in household contacts.
source: We estimate that two- to eightfold increase in viral load level observed with variants of concern could lead to an increase in the probability of transmission by 24–58% in household contacts.

claim: The trial was conducted between March 17 and April 28, 2020 in three out of nine health-care areas in Catalonia, Spain.
source: The trial was conducted between March, 17 and April 28, 2020 in three out of nine health-care area in Catalonia, Spain.

claim: All index cases were individuals aged 18 years or older with nasopharyngeal PCR positive results at baseline and mild symptoms onset within 5 days of inclusion.
source: All index cases were individuals aged 18 years or older, identified by the Catalan epidemiological surveillance system, with no hospitalisation, nasopharyngeal PCR positive results at baseline and mild symptoms onset within 5 days of inclusion and had no reported symptoms of SARS-CoV-2 infections in their accommodation or workplace within the 14 days before enrolment.

claim: High-risk contacts were adults with a recent history of exposure (>15 min within 2 m up to 7 days before enrolment) and absence of COVID-19 like symptoms within the 14 days preceding enrolment.
source: High-risk contacts were adults with a recent history of exposure (i.e. >15 min within 2 m up to 7 days before enrolment) and absence of COVID-19 like symptoms within the 14 days preceding enrolment, and who had an increased risk of infection (e.g. health care worker a household contact, a nursing-home worker, or a nursing-home resident).

claim: Contacts were quarantined upon enrolment to the study.
source: Contacts were quarantined upon enrolment to the study.

claim: Three index individuals and their corresponding 25 contacts were excluded because no viral load data was available.
source: In the original study, 282 index cases and the resulting 753 contacts were enrolled (Marks et al., 2021); here we did not include three index individuals (and their corresponding 25 contacts) for which no viral load data was available, eight index individuals (19 contacts) for which no viral load was detected at any time point, and 12 index cases (127 contacts) for which no date of contact was available.

claim: Eight index individuals and 19 contacts were excluded because no viral load was detected at any time point.
source: In the original study, 282 index cases and the resulting 753 contacts were enrolled (Marks et al., 2021); here we did not include three index individuals (and their corresponding 25 contacts) for which no viral load data was available, eight index individuals (19 contacts) for which no viral load was detected at any time point, and 12 index cases (127 contacts) for which no date of contact was available.

claim: Twelve index cases and 127 contacts were excluded because no date of contact was available.
source: In the original study, 282 index cases and the resulting 753 contacts were enrolled (Marks et al., 2021); here we did not include three index individuals (and their corresponding 25 contacts) for which no viral load data was available, eight index individuals (19 contacts) for which no viral load was detected at any time point, and 12 index cases (127 contacts) for which no date of contact was available.

claim: In 12 index cases, the date of symptoms onset was not known and was imputed to 4 days before their first swab sampling.
source: In 12 index cases, the date of symptoms onset was not known and was imputed to 4 days before their first swab sampling, which corresponds to the median value observed in the population study.

claim: The proportion of infectious virus µ was assumed constant over time and was fixed to 10^-4 as observed in animal model.
source: The proportion of infectious virus µ was assumed constant over time and was fixed to 10−4 as observed in animal model (Gonçalves et al., 2021).

claim: At the moment of infection there was exactly one productively infected cell in the upper respiratory tract.
source: We assumed that at the moment of infection there was exactly one productively infected cell in the upper respiratory tract.

claim: 90% of individuals have an incubation period varying between 4 and 6 days.
source: We assumed that the incubation period was lognormally distributed around 5 days before symptoms onset with a standard deviation of 0.125 days, corresponding to 90% of individuals having an incubation period varying between 4 and 6 days (Jones et al., 2021; Lauer et al., 2020).

claim: Parameter estimations were performed using non-linear mixed-effect model.
source: Parameter estimations were performed using non-linear mixed-effect model.

claim: All parameters were estimated by computing the maximum-likelihood estimator using the stochastic approximation expectation-maximization (SAEM) algorithm implemented in Monolix Software 2020R1.
source: All parameters were estimated by computing the maximum-likelihood estimator using the stochastic approximation expectation-maximization (SAEM) algorithm implemented in Monolix Software 2020R1 (http://www.lixoft.eu/) (Comets et al., 2017; Delyon et al., 1999; Monolix version 2020R1, 2019).
evidence: Statement about statistical methods with citations

claim: All simulations were performed using the Simulx package on R.3.6.0.
source: All simulations were performed using the Simulx package on R.3.6.0.

claim: The transmission probability as large as 48% when the viral load was greater than 10^10 copies per mL in household contacts.
source: The effect of viral load was larger in household contacts than in non-household contacts, with a transmission probability as large as 48% when the viral load was greater than 1010 copies per mL.
evidence: Summary of main finding from abstract

claim: The transmission probability peaked at symptom onset, with a mean probability of transmission of 29%, with large individual variations.
source: The transmission probability peaked at symptom onset, with a mean probability of transmission of 29%, with large individual variations.
evidence: Summary of main finding from abstract

claim: Viral load is increased by two- to eightfold with variants of concern.
source: Based on the current knowledge that viral load is increased by two- to eightfold with variants of concern and assuming no changes in the pattern of contacts across variants, the model predicts that larger viral load levels could lead to a relative increase in the probability of transmission of 24% to 58% in household contacts, and of 15% to 39% in non-household contacts.
evidence: Statement about variants from abstract based on literature

claim: Larger viral load levels could lead to a relative increase in the probability of transmission of 24% to 58% in household contacts for variants of concern.
source: Based on the current knowledge that viral load is increased by two- to eightfold with variants of concern and assuming no changes in the pattern of contacts across variants, the model predicts that larger viral load levels could lead to a relative increase in the probability of transmission of 24% to 58% in household contacts, and of 15% to 39% in non-household contacts.

claim: Larger viral load levels could lead to a relative increase in the probability of transmission of 15% to 39% in non-household contacts for variants of concern.
source: Based on the current knowledge that viral load is increased by two- to eightfold with variants of concern and assuming no changes in the pattern of contacts across variants, the model predicts that larger viral load levels could lead to a relative increase in the probability of transmission of 24% to 58% in household contacts, and of 15% to 39% in non-household contacts.
